title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 52:13–53:12)
hook: a servant despised, wounded, bearing others' griefs; Christians see Jesus here, Jewish readers often Israel

segments.voice: Yesterday, called by name, and your line was you are mine. Whose name did you use on purpose? Day four hundred seventy.

A chariot is rolling slowly down the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. In it sits an official of the queen of Ethiopia, her treasurer, heading home after worshiping in Jerusalem. He's reading aloud from a scroll of Isaiah, the way people read in those days. A man named Philip runs up alongside and hears him. In the King James words of the book of Acts, Philip asks: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" And the official says, how can I, unless someone guides me? Then he asks the question people have been asking about this passage ever since: "of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man?" Today, the passage he was reading.
screen: `A CHARIOT ON THE GAZA ROAD.` → `AN ETHIOPIAN READS ISAIAH.` → `OF WHOM SPEAKETH THE PROPHET?`

segments.voice: Isaiah describes a figure he calls the servant. Not handsome, not impressive; people look away from him. In the King James Bible: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." Then the voice in the poem, a we, has a shock of realization. We thought he was being punished by God. We were wrong. "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows." And then: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." Stripes are the marks of a whip. The healing comes through his wounds. "All we like sheep have gone astray." He is led like a lamb to the slaughter and does not open his mouth. And yet the poem ends with him lifted up, seeing light. So, the Ethiopian's question. Who is he? Christians, from the beginning, have answered: Jesus. In Acts, Philip starts from this very passage and tells the official about Jesus, and he asks to be baptized in the next water they pass. The New Testament echoes these lines again and again, and many churches read them on Good Friday. Jewish interpreters have most often read the servant as Israel itself, a people suffering among the nations, since Isaiah elsewhere calls Israel my servant; some have read him as the prophet, or a righteous few. Both readings are old, and both are held seriously. And a fact worth knowing: among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a nearly complete copy of Isaiah, made well before Jesus was born, with this chapter in it.
screen: `DESPISED AND REJECTED.` · `WE THOUGHT HE WAS PUNISHED.` · `WOUNDED FOR OUR TRANSGRESSIONS.` · `JESUS, OR ISRAEL?` · then, large: `WITH HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who carries other people's pain. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone like that: a nurse, a caregiver, a parent sitting up with a sick child, a friend everyone calls in a crisis, someone carrying grief that isn't even theirs. Picture their shoulders. Notice how much they hold that nobody sees. Stay with them for a while, without rushing to fix anything. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for the strength they need tonight. The bell holds the time.
The suffering servant. Isaiah's despised and wounded figure who carries others' griefs: Jesus, for Christians; most often Israel, for Jewish readers.
Your line: by his stripes. Today, lighten one person's load: take a task off a caregiver, sit with someone tired, or carry something heavy for someone else. Day four hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Christians read Isaiah 52:13–53:12 on Good Friday in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and many Protestant churches, and lines from it are sung in Handel's Messiah and in many Passion hymns.

fork.setup: you're the Ethiopian official, reading a scroll you don't understand, and a stranger offers to explain. what do you do?
options: say no thanks and keep reading.
invite him up into the chariot.

fork.reveal: he invites Philip to sit with him, asks of whom speaketh the prophet this?, and by the end asks to be baptized at the next water.

original.note: Hebrew: a man of sorrows, of pains.

trapdoor: what you thought: a passage that has only ever been read one way.
what it means: a poem of a servant, despised and wounded, who bears others' griefs and is lifted up at the end. Christians read Jesus; Jewish readers most often Israel.
what a scholar hears: one of four servant songs in Isaiah 40–55. the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied around the second century BC, preserves it almost entire.

notes: Readings presented without ranking: Christian (Jesus; Acts 8:35, 1 Peter 2:22–25) and Jewish (most often Israel, e.g. Rashi; also the prophet or the righteous remnant). Confirm fair to both traditions; a Jewish scholar's check is advised.
Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), dated c. 150–100 BC, contains Isaiah 53 nearly complete. Confirm 'nearly complete copy' and the dating.
'Copied around the second century BC' in the trapdoor. Confirm.
The Ethiopian official served the Candace (Acts 8:27), a royal title of the queen of Kush/'Ethiopia'. Confirm 'queen of Ethiopia' as a plain-language rendering.

Audit (10% sample): 'Christians read them every Good Friday' overstated; softened to 'many churches'. Trapdoor's first floor made the Christian reading the naive 'what you thought'; now the naive view is that the passage has only one reading, which the day corrects without ranking either.
